strengths: Clear and well-motivated empirical observation ('shift-readapt-overfit' progression) that explains why SFT-then-RL can underperform pure RL, providing useful insight into training dynamics when off-policy expert data diverges strongly from the model's established policy.
The proposed dual-control mechanism (global coefficient µ + token-wise weighting function ϕ) is simple, interpretable, and easy to implement within a standard GRPO-style pipeline.

The parabolic weighting function ϕ(pt)=pt(1-pt) is intuitively motivated by an uncertainty/entropy argument and empirically shown to mitigate both entropy collapse (from plain IS) and entropy blow-up (from unweighted mixing).

Reasonably comprehensive experiments spanning two different tasks (math reasoning and tool-use) and two different base models, with a good set of baselines (SFT-only, RL-only, SFT+RL, SASR, LUFFY) plus multiple ablations (fixed vs. decayed µ, with/without ϕ, warmup-decay schedule) and qualitative case studies showing behavioral differences.

Useful supplementary analysis distinguishing off-policy effects on base vs. instruction-tuned models, which clarifies the paper's specific and underexplored setting (fine-tuning an already well-aligned instruct model with off-policy experts).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: reweighting SFT loss and dynamically scheduling its coefficient during RL builds directly on ideas already explored in cited works (LUFFY, SRFT, SASR, In-RIL, iw-SFT/DFT); the core technical contribution (a symmetric p(1-p) token weight and a linear/exponential µ decay) is fairly simple and not deeply justified theoretically beyond an informal entropy/uncertainty argument.

Comparisons to the most relevant recent baseline, SRFT, are only discussed qualitatively in related work but not included in the main experimental comparison, weakening the empirical positioning against the closest competing method.
The LUFFY baseline is trained with less data (20k vs. its original 45k) due to the authors' setup, which could unfairly disadvantage this baseline and makes the comparison less controlled.

Gains over strong baselines are sometimes small or mixed (e.g., CHORD-φ underperforms CHORD-µ on AIME25; CHORD-µ underperforms SFT-best+RL on MMLU-Pro), and it is unclear whether the differences are statistically significant given the relatively small benchmark sizes (e.g., AIME24/25 have only 30 problems) and apparent single-seed reporting for most tables.

Experiments are limited to two backbone models (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and LLaMA3.2-3B-Instruct) and two task domains; scalability to larger models or more diverse tasks (e.g., open-ended generation, code) is untested, limiting evidence for general applicability.

The token-wise weighting function is only compared against plain IS and no-IS ablations; no comparison to alternative principled weighting schemes (e.g., entropy-based, confidence-based, or learned weighting) is provided to justify the specific choice of p(1-p) beyond its intuitive appeal.

Hyperparameter sensitivity (e.g., decay rate/shape for µ, fixed µ value used with ϕ) is only partially explored, and the practical recipe for selecting these values across new tasks is not clearly specified, which may hinder reproducibility.

The tool-use experiments use a very small SFT set (500 examples) and only single-turn ToolAce instances, raising questions about how well the findings generalize to more complex, multi-turn or larger-scale tool-use settings.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically relevant and timely problem: how to combine off-policy expert (SFT) data with on-policy RL for LLM post-training, specifically in the under-explored setting of starting from an already instruction-tuned model rather than a base model.
The 'shift-readapt-overfit' empirical analysis (Fig. 2) and the entropy-collapse-with-IS observation (Fig. 5) provide useful, intuitive motivation for the proposed dual-control design.

The proposed token-wise weighting function phi(p)=p(1-p) is simple, interpretable, and cheaply computable, and the ablations (fixed vs. decayed mu, with/without phi) are reasonably thorough and illustrate the mechanism's effect on entropy and reward.

Experiments span two different task types (math reasoning and tool-use) and two different model families/sizes, together with several relevant baselines (SASR, LUFFY, SFT+RL variants), which is a non-trivial empirical effort.

The paper includes useful supplementary analyses (response-length dynamics, detailed per-category BFCL/MMLU-Pro tables, base-vs-instruct model comparison, and qualitative case studies) that add some transparency to the claims.
weaknesses: Core novelty is incremental: convex combination of SFT and RL losses with a global coefficient (Eq. 3) is essentially the same idea as several cited works (SRFT, interleaved SFT/RL, SASR), and the paper's own related-work section only distinguishes itself by the 'starting from an instruct model instead of base model' framing, which is a narrow and somewhat superficial differentiator rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The token-wise weighting phi(p)=p(1-p) is motivated informally (entropy/uncertainty heuristic) without any theoretical justification connecting it to the actual objective being optimized (e.g., no derivation showing this is optimal or even principled beyond analogy to Bernoulli variance); the IS formulation in Eq. 4 also makes a strong and under-justified assumption (behavior policy probability =1), which is just asserted via 'common practice' citation.

Experimental scale is limited: math experiments use only 7B/1.5B models and a single training seed per configuration (error bars shown in some plots but not consistently reported in main Table 1); AIME24/25 and AMC are small benchmarks with inherently high variance, and no statistical significance testing is provided despite close performance gaps (e.g., CHORD-µ vs SFT-best+RL AIME25: 17.9 vs 16.3).

LUFFY comparison is explicitly handicapped (20k vs. 45k training samples, reproducing lower numbers than the original paper) which undermines the fairness of this key baseline comparison and is only explained in a footnote; LUFFY is also entirely missing from the tool-use evaluation.

The dual-control mechanism's necessity is not cleanly isolated: CHORD-phi uses a fixed mu=0.1 while CHORD-mu uses a decayed schedule, so the comparison between the two does not cleanly ablate the token-wise function alone versus the mu schedule — a rigorous ablation (e.g., decayed mu + phi vs. decayed mu alone) is relegated to Appendix A.3 and shows only a 'slightly better' difference, which raises doubts about how much of the gain is attributable to phi versus simply mu-tuning.

Reward design for math (manually restricting to integer-answer problems, and a specific penalty scheme) and other hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, mu schedule, phi) appear heavily tuned per-task without a clear description of how these were chosen or how sensitive results are to them, raising reproducibility and generalization concerns.

The qualitative case study presented (Appendix D) is a single illustrative example repeated across sections; such anecdotal evidence is weak support for claims about 'hybrid reasoning style' and selective absorption of expert patterns, and could easily be cherry-picked.

The paper's title and framing ('on-policy RL meets off-policy experts') and the overall contribution largely amount to a loss-reweighting trick; given the closely related prior work already cited (SRFT, LUFFY, SASR, UFT, BREAD), the marginal technical and empirical contribution over this already crowded space appears modest for a top-tier venue.

No analysis of computational overhead or wall-clock cost of maintaining both the RL rollout pipeline and the auxiliary SFT forward/backward pass is provided, despite this being relevant to practical adoption claims.

strengths: The paper provides a clear and well-motivated empirical analysis of the 'shift-readapt-overfit' phenomenon when applying SFT with off-policy expert data to instruction-tuned models, which helps explain why the common SFT-then-RL pipeline can underperform pure RL.

The proposed CHORD framework is simple, intuitive, and well-grounded: reframing SFT as a dynamically weighted auxiliary loss within on-policy RL, with a global coefficient µ and a token-wise weighting function ϕ(·) that down-weights both very confident and very uncertain tokens.

The token-wise weighting function ϕ(pt) = pt(1-pt) has a clean information-theoretic interpretation (maximal uncertainty weighting) and is simple to implement, making the method easy to adopt in practice.

Experiments span two distinct domains (math reasoning and tool-use) and multiple benchmarks (AIME24/25, AMC, MMLU-Pro, BFCL), with a reasonably comprehensive set of baselines (SFT-only, RL-only, SFT+RL, LUFFY, SASR).

The paper includes informative ablations and analyses (entropy loss curves, reward curves, response-length dynamics, fixed vs. dynamic µ, joint tuning of µ and ϕ) that help build confidence in the claimed mechanism, along with qualitative case studies showing CHORD-ϕ's hybrid reasoning style.

The explicit positioning versus prior work is clear: the paper correctly identifies that most related methods (LUFFY, SRFT, Reift) start from a base model and argues that starting from an instruction-tuned model poses a distinct and practically important challenge.
weaknesses: The experimental scale is somewhat limited: only one model size per task (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct for math, LLaMA3.2-3B-Instruct for tool-use), so it's unclear whether the results generalize across model scales and families.

Reported results appear to be single-run numbers (aside from avg@32/avg@8 for evaluation variance), with no reported variance/seeds for training runs themselves, especially given RL training is well known to be noisy; this makes it hard to assess the statistical significance of claimed gains (e.g., +1.0-2.4 points over SFT-best+RL on AIME24/AMC).

The comparison with LUFFY uses fewer training samples (20k vs. 45k in the original paper) and tool-use comparison is omitted entirely due to 'incompatible requirements,' which weakens the fairness/completeness of this baseline comparison.

The core weighting function ϕ(pt)=pt(1-pt) is a reasonable but fairly simple heuristic; while the paper acknowledges this is just one instantiation of a general principle, no systematic comparison against alternative instantiations (e.g., entropy-based, different parabolic shapes) is provided to justify this specific choice over plausible alternatives.

The µ decay schedule hyperparameters (e.g., decaying from 0.9 to 0.05 over the first 200 steps, or different schedules for tool-use vs math) appear to require task-specific tuning, which is in some tension with the paper's claim that ϕ(·) 'simplifies practical usage' and reduces sensitivity to µ scheduling — the actual sensitivity analysis is somewhat limited (Appendix A.3 compares only two schedules).

Combining SFT and RL losses in a single batch effectively doubles computational cost per step (forward/backward passes on both expert data and on-policy rollouts), but the paper does not report or discuss computational overhead relative to baselines such as pure RL or SFT-then-RL.

The improvements over the strongest baselines (e.g., SFT-best+RL) on some metrics are relatively modest in absolute terms (e.g., AIME25: 17.2 vs 16.3, or even a slight regression on AIME25 for CHORD-ϕ vs CHORD-µ), raising questions about the practical significance of the method beyond trends.

strengths: Provides a clear and interesting empirical analysis (the 'shift-readapt-overfit' progression) that motivates the proposed method and gives insight into why SFT-then-RL pipelines can underperform pure RL when fine-tuning already-aligned instruct models.

The dual-control mechanism (global coefficient µ for macro-level scheduling and token-wise weighting φ(p)=p(1-p) for micro-level stability) is intuitive, computationally cheap (element-wise multiplication on existing forward-pass probabilities), and well motivated by the entropy-collapse/entropy-explosion trade-off shown in Figure 5.

Extensive experimentation: two distinct task families (math reasoning and tool use), multiple base models (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, LLaMA3.2-3B-Instruct), and a large appendix with many additional studies (adaptive µ, alternative φ variants including entropy-based/focal loss/IS-clip, different expert data sources, non-verifiable domains, weaker policy models, MoE architecture, base vs instruct model comparisons) that substantially strengthen the empirical case.

Comparisons against a comprehensive and relevant set of baselines (SFT-only, SFT+RL, LUFFY, SASR, and in the appendix SRFT), with discussion of why CHORD is particularly suited to the instruct-model fine-tuning setting as opposed to the 'zero-RL' setting most prior work targets.

Qualitative case studies (Appendix E) provide convincing, human-readable evidence that CHORD-φ produces a hybrid reasoning style that blends conciseness with selective adoption of expert verification patterns, supporting the quantitative claims.
Reasonably thorough experimental setup documentation (Appendix A) with hyperparameters, prompts, and reward functions, aiding reproducibility, along with a promise to release code.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: dynamically weighting SFT/RL losses and token-wise reweighting of off-policy signals have been explored in related works (SRFT, LUFFY, SASR, UFT, BREAD); the paper's main differentiator (targeting already-instruction-tuned models rather than base models) is a useful but relatively narrow framing rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

The φ(p)=p(1-p) weighting function, while empirically effective, is a fairly ad hoc heuristic; the 'information-theoretic' justification is thin, and the paper itself acknowledges in Section 4.3 that it is 'unlikely a single universally optimal design exists,' which somewhat undercuts the principledness of the contribution.

Baseline comparisons are not always matched in data budget (e.g., LUFFY is evaluated with fewer training samples than its original paper, and SFT data sizes vary substantially across methods—500 vs 5k for tool-use), which could bias some comparisons in CHORD's favor or make them harder to interpret.

Despite claims that φ(·) reduces sensitivity to µ, the overall framework still involves multiple interacting hyperparameters (µ initial value, decay schedule/steps, fixed µ choice, φ formulation) that require tuning per task, somewhat undermining the 'simplification' claim.

Reported results lack clear variance/statistical significance measures for most tables (aside from avg@32/avg@8 on a few reasoning benchmarks), making it harder to assess whether the (often modest, e.g., +0.1–2.4 point) improvements over strong baselines like GRPO/SFT-best+RL are robust.

The theoretical understanding of why the shift-readapt-overfit dynamic occurs, and why the specific token-wise weighting is optimal, remains largely empirical/qualitative rather than formally grounded, which the authors themselves note as a limitation for future work.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically important and timely problem: how to combine off-policy expert SFT data with on-policy RL exploration when starting from an already instruction-tuned model, which is more realistic for many practitioners than the 'zero-RL' base-model setting studied in most prior work.

The 'shift-readapt-overfit' empirical characterization of SFT training dynamics (Figure 2) is a nice, intuitive observation that motivates the method and is reasonably well supported by the entropy/reward curves shown throughout.

The dual-control design (global coefficient µ + token-wise weighting φ(pt)=pt(1-pt)) is simple, interpretable, and cheap to compute, and the ablations in Appendix B.2 testing alternative token-weighting schemes (entropy-based, IS-clip, focal loss) add some credibility to the specific instantiation chosen.

Reasonably broad empirical coverage: math reasoning and tool-use tasks, different model families/sizes (Qwen2.5-7B, LLaMA3.2-3B, a MoE model, a weaker 3B model), different expert sources, and a non-verifiable domain (RaR-Medicine), which speaks to generalizability.
Reproducibility statement and implementation release claim, plus detailed hyperparameter and prompt documentation in the appendix.
weaknesses: Core novelty is incremental: the idea of dynamically mixing SFT and RL losses (µ term) is essentially a continuous relaxation of interleaved/periodic SFT-RL schedules already explored by SASR, SRFT, and others cited in the paper; the token-wise weighting φ(pt)=pt(1-pt) is a very simple closed-form heuristic (akin to a variance/uncertainty proxy) without deep theoretical grounding, and the general principle (down-weight both very confident and very unlikely tokens) overlaps substantially with existing entropy-based and importance-sampling-based approaches already discussed in the related work.

Baseline comparisons for the main table are not entirely apples-to-apples: the paper explicitly notes in a footnote that LUFFY was evaluated with far fewer training samples (20k vs. 45k for math, 500 vs 5k SFT samples for tool-use) than its original configuration, and SRFT/LUFFY comparisons in Appendix D.1 use different expert-data volumes than CHORD (5000 vs 500), making it hard to disentangle whether gains come from the proposed mechanism or from the altered experimental budget.

Statistical rigor is weak: no variance/confidence intervals or multiple-seed results are reported for the main Table 1 comparisons (only avg@32/avg@8 for individual benchmark evaluation, not for training runs), despite RL training being known to have high run-to-run variance; many of the claimed improvements (e.g., +1.0 AIME24, +0.3 overall BFCL) are numerically small and could plausibly fall within noise.

The method introduces/relies on several additional hyperparameters (µ schedule shape and decay step, φ formulation) whose tuning sensitivity is only partially explored; the µ-only variant (CHORD-µ) is shown to require careful scheduling and is less practical, and while the paper argues φ makes µ 'less critical', this argument rests on a single ablation (Figure 11) with limited settings.

Some claims are asserted rather than rigorously demonstrated: e.g., the interpretation of p(1-p) as 'policy uncertainty' and the claim that this creates a principled 'learning sweet spot' is intuitively plausible but not theoretically justified or connected to a formal objective (e.g., no derivation connecting it to any variance-reduction or regret bound).

The experimental settings are relatively small-scale (7B and smaller models, limited step budgets, e.g., 100 steps for tool-use RL), raising questions about whether conclusions generalize to larger models or longer training regimes typical of state-of-the-art LLM post-training pipelines.

Related work positioning versus SRFT, LUFFY, and SASR is somewhat defensive/post-hoc (e.g., Appendix D.1 argues these are 'zero-RL' methods not designed for the instruct-model setting), but this framing conveniently sidesteps the fact that the core technical contribution (dynamic mixing coefficient + token reweighting) is conceptually similar to ideas already present in SRFT's sample-level SFT weighting and LUFFY's importance-sampling reweighting.
Figures throughout (e.g., Fig 1, 2, 4-13) lack error bars or seed information, and some key quantitative claims (e.g., 'shift-readapt' phase boundaries) are described qualitatively from a single run.

strengths: The paper provides a clear and well-motivated empirical analysis of why sequential SFT-then-RL often underperforms pure RL, identifying the 'shift-readapt-overfit' progression, which gives useful intuition for the proposed method.

CHORD's dual-control design (global coefficient µ for macro-level scheduling and token-wise weighting ϕ(p)=p(1-p) for micro-level control) is simple, interpretable, and computationally cheap, requiring only existing forward-pass probabilities.

The experimental evaluation is unusually extensive: it spans math reasoning and tool-use tasks, multiple models (Qwen2.5-7B/3B, LLaMA3.2-3B, a Phi MoE model), multiple expert data sources, non-verifiable domains (medical QA), and weaker policy models, lending good support to the generality of the claims.

Thorough ablations are provided, including comparisons against several alternative token-weighting schemes (entropy-based, IS-clip, focal loss), adaptive µ schedules, and a dedicated comparison with strong recent baselines (LUFFY, SRFT, SASR) under matched instruct-model settings, with an honest discussion of why these zero-RL-oriented baselines underperform in the instruct-tuning setting.

The paper is transparent about limitations of its own baselines (e.g., noting when LUFFY uses fewer samples than its original paper) and provides qualitative case studies that meaningfully illustrate the differences in reasoning style produced by each method.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental: mixing an SFT loss into on-policy RL with a scheduled coefficient and token-level reweighting is conceptually similar to several cited works (SRFT, LUFFY, interleaved SFT/RL methods, importance-sampling-based SFT); the main new element is the specific ϕ(p)=p(1-p) instantiation, whose justification is heuristic/informal rather than rigorously derived.

No variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported for the main training runs (Table 1), despite RL training being known to be high-variance; this makes it hard to assess whether the reported gains (often a few points) are statistically robust.

Model scale is limited to 1.5B–7B parameter models; it remains unclear whether the shift-readapt-overfit phenomenon and the benefits of CHORD persist at larger, more capable model scales typical of current frontier LLMs.

Despite claims that ϕ(·) reduces sensitivity to µ, the method still requires tuning a fixed or scheduled µ value and a reward threshold for adaptive variants, so the practical hyperparameter burden is not fully eliminated.

Some baseline comparisons may be undertuned relative to CHORD (e.g., LUFFY/SRFT were originally designed and tuned for base-model zero-RL settings, and sample budgets differ from their original papers), which, despite being disclosed, complicates strictly fair comparison.

The paper's main text addresses only two task domains with relatively small/mid-size models and limited benchmark diversity (e.g., no broader open-ended instruction-following or safety-alignment evaluation), slightly limiting the demonstrated scope of impact despite claims of general applicability.
